<margin>Su Commentary <note>Su Zhe, 1039 to 1112, a prominent Song Dynasty scholar</note></margin>Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but devote themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily. Without a single principle to unify this knowledge, they cannot avoid it becoming a burden. Confucius said: Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it. This is the second level of knowledge. If one day you know the Way, you will look back on worldly deceptions and realize that all is false. By removing the false and returning to your true nature, this is what is called "decreasing." Confucius asked his disciple Zigong: Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all? Zigong replied: Yes, is it not so? Confucius said: No, I permeate everything with a single principle. To forget the worldly mind and restore one's nature is called decreasing. As long as delusions remain, one must continue this process until even the act of forgetting is forgotten. When the mind is pure and nature is restored without remainder, one removes "doing" and reaches the state of "non-doing" <note>original: <term>wu wei</term></note>. People all have the desire to take hold of the world and manage its affairs. Because they create complications and seek external results, their intentions are visible, and things resist them; thus, they encounter difficulty and fail. The Sage practices non-doing, so his mind has no worldly affairs. His inner state is visible externally, and things are at peace with him. Though he does not strive to take the world or manage its affairs, the world and its affairs naturally follow and find peace.

<margin>Lü Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032 to 1111, a key political figure and philosopher</note></margin>To pursue learning is the path for those who have not yet heard the Way. Because they seek it without knowing it, they must be broad in their study; thus it is said to "increase." To pursue the Way is for those who have already heard it. Because they act upon what they know, they must practice non-doing; thus it is said to "decrease." To "decrease and further decrease" refers to those who have not yet escaped purposeful action. One must decrease even the act of decreasing itself to finally reach the state of non-doing. Non-doing means remaining silent and unmoving. "Doing nothing left undone" means that when stimulated, one resonates and connects with all circumstances under heaven. To reach non-doing through the act of non-doing is the constant path. Learning without worry is called divine. The direction of the divine is the Way. Who can attain such supreme divinity? From this we see that to take the world, one must always use non-doing. If one relies on purposeful action, it is clear that such a person is not fit to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai Commentary <note>Huang Maocai, a Southern Song Dynasty scholar</note></margin>Only after one reaches a state of knowing everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires a daily increase. Only after one reaches a state of doing nothing can one speak of the Way; therefore, the Way desires a daily decrease. However, "increase" can be pursued through progress, while "decrease" is often difficult to achieve through forced effort. Only those with supreme clarity can suddenly cast off worldly attachments and reach the realm of non-doing. Thus, they can leave nothing undone, and their applications are inexhaustible, spreading through the world with great ease.

<margin>Xizhai Commentary <note>Li Daochun, a 13th century Taoist master whose literary name was Xizhai</note></margin>The purpose of learning is to seek knowledge, hence the daily increase. The purpose of the Way is to remove delusion, hence the daily decrease. If knowledge is not perfected, the decrease will not be complete. Therefore, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, one reaches non-doing. Upon reaching non-doing, any purposeful action is itself non-doing. This state cannot easily be discussed in terms of mere increase or decrease. When non-doing reaches its peak, though the world is vast, it is unified by a single principle. If one uses busy-ness to create more business, life becomes difficult and lacks leisure. If even a single object can cause entanglement and error, how much more so the vastness of the world?

<margin>Commentary by Su</margin> Not knowing yet striving for knowledge, seeing and hearing more each day without a way to unify it, one cannot avoid being burdened. Confucius said: "Hear much, select the good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second tier of knowledge." If one truly understands the Way, then one sees that all false actions are vanity. Removing vanity to return to one's true nature is what is meant by "diminishing." Confucius asked Zigong: "Do you think that I am a person who learns much and remembers it?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with a single thread." To forget the grasping mind in order to purely return to one's true nature, this is what is meant by diminishing. If one does not stop at forgetting the mind, but also lets go of that very forgetting to achieve a state of pure, natural existence with nothing left over, only then can one engage in action without losing the essence of non-action. People all have desires and the intent to grasp the affairs and principles of the world. Thus, they create affairs and seek them; their minds are revealed externally, and things resist them, making success impossible. The Sage practices non-action, so there are no affairs; his mind is not revealed externally, and things are at peace. Though he does not seek to grasp the affairs and principles of the world, they are practiced, and the affairs and principles of the world are then harmonious and at peace.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin> To study is to seek the Way without yet having heard it. If one has not heard the Way and seeks it, one must be broad in learning, hence it is said "to increase daily." To practice the Way is to have already heard it. If one has already heard the Way and acts upon it, one must inevitably arrive at non-action, hence it is said "diminish and diminish again" because one has not yet avoided having a sense of action. By diminishing even that sense of diminishing, one finally arrives at true non-action. Non-action is a state of stillness and lack of movement. "Doing nothing, yet leaving nothing undone" means responding to all things in the world and being connected to their fundamental patterns. To move from non-action to the ultimate state of non-action is what is meant by the classics. Learning without anxiety is called spirit. The method of the spirit is the Way. Who can reach this state of supreme spirit? Viewing it from this perspective, we can understand why those who seek to govern the world through constant, calculated action are insufficient to take possession of the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin> Only after one knows everything can one speak of learning, hence learning seeks to increase daily. Only after one can do everything can one speak of the Way, hence the Way seeks to diminish daily. However, "increasing" allows one to advance in seeking, while "diminishing" may be difficult to force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly cast off their attachments and arrive at the realm of non-action. Thus, they are able to perform all actions, and their applications are inexhaustible, governing the world with ease and abundance.

reference: Kung-nî said, 'Once when I was sent on a mission to Khû, I saw some pigs sucking at their dead mother. After a little they looked with rapid glances, when they all left her, and ran away. They felt that she did not see them, and that she was no longer like themselves. What they had loved in their mother was not her bodily figure, but what had given animation to her figure. When a man dies in battle, they do not at his interment employ the usual appendages of plumes: as to supplying shoes to one who has lost his feet, there is no reason why he should care for them;—in neither case is there the proper reason for their use. The members of the royal harem do not pare their nails nor pierce their ears; when a man is newly married, he remains (for a time) absent from his official duties, and unoccupied with them. That their bodies might be perfect was sufficient to make them thus dealt with;—how much greater results should be expected from men whose mental gifts are perfect!

<margin>Feeding at the breast</margin>
The child feeding at the breast of its dead mother, after a short while, looks as if it has lost her, and <margin>This means that at the blink of an eye, the mother is gone</margin>
rising, it does not see her. It does not find anyone who resembles her. That which you loved in your mother was <margin>The stiffening of the body no longer resembles her</margin>

10. Confucius said, 'The minds of men are more difficult of approach than (the position defended by) mountains and rivers, and more difficult to know than Heaven itself. Heaven has its periods of spring and autumn, of winter and summer, and of morning and evening; but man's exterior is thickly veiled, and his feelings lie deep. Thus the demeanour of some is honest-like, and yet they go to excess (in what is mean); others are really gifted, and yet look to be without ability; some seem docile and impressible, but yet they have far-reaching schemes; others look firm, and yet may be twisted about; others look slow, and yet they are hasty. In this way those who hasten to do what is right as if they were thirsty will anon hurry away from it as if it were fire. Hence the superior man looks at them when employed at a distance to test their fidelity, and when employed near at hand to test their reverence. By employing them on difficult services, he tests their ability; by questioning them suddenly, he tests their knowledge; by appointing them a fixed time, he tests their good faith; by entrusting them with wealth, he tests their benevolence; by telling them of danger, he tests their self-command in emergencies; by making them drunk, he tests their tendencies; by placing them in a variety of society, he tests their chastity: -- by these nine tests the inferior man is discovered.'

11. When Khao-fu, the Correct, received the first grade of official rank, he walked with head bowed down; on receiving the second, with bent back; on receiving the third, with body stooping, he ran and hurried along the wall: -- who would presume not to take him as a model? But one of those ordinary men, on receiving his first appointment, goes along with a haughty stride; on receiving his second, he looks quite elated in his chariot; and on receiving the third, he calls his uncles by their personal names; -- how very different from Hsü (Yû) in the time (of Yâo of) Thang!

Of all things that injure (men) there is none greater than the practising of virtue with the purpose of the mind, till the mind becomes supercilious. When it becomes so, the mind (only) looks inwards (on itself), and such looking into itself leads to its ruin. This evil quality has five forms, and the chief of them is that which is the central. What do we mean by the central quality? It is that which appears in a man's loving (only) his own views, and reviling whatever he does not do (himself).

There may be similarity in understanding without similarity in outward form. There may also be similarity in form without similarity in understanding. The Sage embraces similarity of understanding and pays no regard to similarity of form. The world in general is attracted by similarity of form, but remains indifferent to similarity of understanding. Those creatures that resemble them in shape they love and consort with; those that differ from them in shape they fear and keep at a distance. The creature that has a skeleton seven feet long, hands differently shaped from the feet, hair on its head, and an even set of teeth in its jaws, and walks erect, is called a man. But it does not follow that a man may not have the mind of a brute. Even though this be the case, other men will still recognise him as one of their own species in virtue of his outward form. Creatures which have wings on the back or horns on the head, serrated teeth or extensile talons, which fly overhead or run on all fours, are called birds and beasts. But it does not follow that a bird or a beast may not have the mind of a man. Yet, even if this be so, it is nevertheless assigned to another species because of the difference in form. P'ao Hsi, Nü Kua, Shen Nung and Hsia Hou had serpents' bodies, human faces, ox-heads and tigers' snouts. Thus, their forms were not human, yet their virtue was of the saintliest. Chieh of the Hsia dynasty, Chou of the Yin, Huan of the Lu State, and Mu of the Ch'u State, were in all external respects, as facial appearance and possession of the seven channels of sense, like unto other men; yet they had the minds of savage brutes. Howbeit, in seeking perfect wisdom, men attend to the outward form alone, which will not bring them near to it.

When the Yellow Emperor fought with Yen Ti on the field of P'an-ch'uan, his vanguard was composed of bears, wolves, panthers, lynxes and tigers, while his ensign-bearers were eagles, ospreys, falcons and kites. This was forcible impressment of animals into the service of man. The Emperor Yao entrusted K'uei with the regulation of music. When the latter tapped the musical stone in varying cadence, all the animals danced to the sound of the music. When the strains of the Shao were heard on the flute, the phoenix itself flew down to assist. This was the attraction of animals by the power of music.

The sophists common to-day say: "Ch'ie and Chou were the legal rulers of the empire; T'ang and Wu rebelled and took it by force." This is not so. If by being Emperor is meant that Ch'ie and Chou possessed the registers and census records of the empire at that time, then yes. If it means that they themselves possessed the empire, then no. If it means that the empire could be said to be in the hands of Ch'ie and Chou, then no. In ancient times the Emperor had a thousand officials, and the feudal princes a hundred officials. By being king is meant to have his command performed through the states of China through these thousand officials. By being prince is meant to have his command performed throughout his borders through those hundred officials, and although his state be not at peace, yet not to be cast aside, displaced and ruined. The descendants of the Sage-Kings inherited the empire; the authority and the registers were in their hands. But if the Imperial Clan of the Empire had not a man of ability, it was unfit for its position. On the one hand his subjects hated him, and on the other the feudal princes revolted. Near the capital, those within his own borders were not united; at a distance, the feudal princes did not obey. His commands were not performed within his own borders. The feudal princes even invaded and sliced off some of his territory; they attacked and chastised him. When such was the situation, although he had not yet fallen, I say that he did not truly possess the empire. When the Sage-Kings died, those who possessed the authority and registers became weak, and became unable to control the empire.

When the country has no real prince, if there is a feudal noble who has ability, and if his virtue is illustrious and his majesty is great, none of the people of the country will be unwilling to take him for prince and leader; then if he should seek out and kill this isolated and wasteful tyrant, he would not injure anyone, he would be a blameless subject. If he put to death the prince of a tyrannous state, it would be the same as killing an ordinary individual. A person like this can be said to be able to wield the empire. He who is able to wield the empire can be called a King. T'ang and Wu did not capture the empire; they cultivated their ways (Tao); they carried out the principle of justice (Yi); they exalted the common benefit of the Empire; they did away with the common sources of injury to the empire; and so the empire turned to them. Ch'ie and Chou did not resign the empire; they perverted the virtue of Yu and T'ang; they confused the distinctions of the rules of proper conduct (Li) and justice (Yi); their bestial actions heaped up misfortune for them, completed their evil destiny, and the empire dismissed them. He to whom the empire turns is called King; he whom the empire dismisses, is ruined. In ancient times, the Son of Heaven <note>the Emperor</note> had a thousand officials and the feudal lords had a hundred officials. When a ruler used these thousand officials to ensure his orders were carried out across all the Chinese states, he was called a King. However, if he is untalented and lacks integrity <gloss>literally "not hitting the mark," meaning not upright</gloss>, then internally the common people will hate him, and externally the feudal lords will rebel against him. Those nearby within his borders will not be unified, and the distant feudal lords will not obey. His orders will not even be carried out within his own territory. In extreme cases, the feudal lords will seize and diminish his lands or launch military attacks against him. In such a state, even if he has not yet perished, I say he no longer possesses the world.

When a Sage King dies and his successor is weak and incapable of managing affairs <gloss>literally "tired" or "weak," meaning unable to hold things together</gloss>, he cannot bind the world to him. If the world is without a true ruler, and there is a feudal lord whose virtue is bright and whose prestige has accumulated so that all the people within the four seas wish to have him as their ruler and teacher—yet a violent state remains arrogant and willful—then that lord must punish them. He will certainly not harm innocent people. Punishing the ruler of a violent state is like punishing a solitary fellow <gloss>meaning a man who has lost all support and stands alone</gloss>. The first four and the latter three subtle marks are, according to the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*, Volume One, identical to this. This first section matches the three and four within the coarse marks, totaling six; thus, these names are borrowed to categorize these six.

○ 1. The mark of attachment and grasping to names.

The first is "attachment-correspondence defilement," which is abandoned by the two vehicles upon liberation and by those at the stage of faith-correspondence. This corresponds to the third and fourth of the six coarse marks. It is also the meaning of the increase of views and desires of the aforementioned consciousness; it is also the aspect of "discriminated attachment" among the four marks mentioned above. Since the coarse mind externally attaches and corresponds to objects, polluting pure practice, it is called "defiled." Liberation of the two vehicles refers to reaching the stage of no-more-learning, where the defilements of view and practice are completely abandoned. "Faith-correspondence" refers to the ten stages of understanding and beyond, where the root of faith is perfected and never lost; thus, it is called faith-correspondence. The *Treatise on the Ten Stages* states that all stages before the actual stages are collectively called the "stage of faith-practice." The *Treatise on Non-Attachment* says the same. This Bodhisattva

The *Summary of the Mahayana* states that if one does not cut off the higher mind, one is no different from an ordinary person; if one does not retain the seeds of defilement, one is no different from the two vehicles. Moreover, there are two intentions for retaining defilement: for oneself and for others. This is explained according to the Final Teaching. If it were according to the Initial Teaching, the retention of defilement is only spoken of from the first stage upward, as stated in other treatises. This Bodhisattva does not only cut off the four dwellings and human attachment, but also partially cuts off the dwelling of ignorance. Therefore, this treatise says later, "those who do not understand the meaning of the one Dharma-realm." Because one observes and learns to cut it off from the stage of faith-correspondence, for the sake of clarifying the coarseness of the attachment to a human self, the other is not discussed here.

○ 2. The mark of continuity.

The second is "uninterrupted-correspondence defilement," which depends on the stage of faith-correspondence, where one studies and practices skillful means, gradually letting it go, and finally abandoning it completely at the stage of pure-mind-ground.
*Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*, Volume One, is the same.
This is the second of the six coarse marks. From this one to the sixth, they are matched in reverse to the five consciousnesses mentioned earlier; this is the fifth in that position. Simply grasping at the continuity of dharma, where birth and death arise without cessation, is the meaning of "continuity." The Lord Buddha addressed Subhuti, saying: "What think you? If a benevolent person bestowed as alms, an abundance of the seven treasures sufficient to fill the universe, would there accrue to that person a considerable merit?"

Regarding the second, the characteristic of continuity, the phrase "depends upon consciousness" explains the basis for its arising. That is to say, based on the aforementioned discrimination, one experiences pleasure upon encountering desirable objects and experiences suffering upon encountering undesirable objects. Through the repeated generation of thoughts, this continuity manifests before us. This explains the internal continuity. Furthermore, it gives rise to defilements that nourish karma, thereby attracting and maintaining the cycle of birth and death, which in turn causes the continuity of others. As the following text says, it "maintains suffering and pleasure, and so on." Therefore, the text states, "it gives rise to... until it is uninterrupted."

The third is the characteristic of clinging. This refers to the failure to understand that the aforementioned objects of suffering and pleasure are empty and non-existent, leading one to deeply grasp at them.

<summary>This passage explains the second and third stages of mental evolution in the context of the Awakening of Faith, specifically focusing on the continuous flow of consciousness driven by emotional responses and the subsequent deep attachment to perceived objects.</summary>
<keywords>Continuity, Consciousness, Suffering and Pleasure, Karma, Birth and Death, Clinging, Empty, Discrimination</keywords>
translations.T2:
The second is the aspect of continuity, which depends on knowledge <note>original: 智, referring to the faculty of discernment or discriminatory consciousness</note>. Because of the arising of the perception of suffering and joy, thoughts emerge and continue without interruption.

Regarding the second, the aspect of continuity, the dependence on knowledge means that, based on the aforementioned discrimination, one arises a feeling of joy when encountering desired objects and a feeling of suffering when encountering undesired objects. Thoughts emerge repeatedly and the continuity becomes manifest. This explains the self-continuity. Furthermore, it can give rise to afflictions <term>klesha</term> <gloss>mental defilements</gloss> that nourish actions and draw one into the cycle of birth and death, which also causes the continuity of others. The text below mentions the sustaining of suffering and joy, and so on. Therefore, it is said that it gives rise to these, continuing until there is no interruption.

The third is the aspect of attachment, which means that, regarding the aforementioned objects of suffering and joy, one does not understand their emptiness and deeply gives rise to attachment.

<summary>This passage defines the aspects of continuity and attachment within the context of Buddhist consciousness, explaining how discriminatory knowledge leads to cyclical suffering through the interaction of perception, emotion, and desire.</summary>
<keywords>continuity, suffering, joy, attachment, mental defilements, birth and death, emptiness</keywords>
translations.T3:
Second: The phase of continuity. This relies on the function of intellectual cognition <term>zhi</term> <gloss>the wisdom that distinguishes</gloss>. It generates the feeling-mind of suffering and pleasure, giving rise to thoughts that are associated and uninterrupted.

Regarding the explanation of this continuity as relying on intellectual cognition: this clarifies that which the continuity depends upon for its arising. Specifically, it relies on the previous discrimination between desirable objects, which gives rise to the perception of pleasure, and undesirable objects, which gives rise to the perception of suffering. These thoughts arise repeatedly, appearing one after another in a continuous stream. This explains the internal continuity of the self. Furthermore, it can give rise to afflictions <term>huo</term> <gloss>klesha or delusions</gloss> which nourish karma and sustain the cycle of birth and death <term>shengsi</term> <gloss>samsara</gloss>. This causes the continuity of the other <note>referring to the chain of future rebirths</note>. As the later text states: it maintains and supports suffering and pleasure. Therefore, the text says it generates feelings up to the point of being uninterrupted.

Third: The phase of grasping. This refers to the aforementioned realms of suffering and pleasure. Because one does not understand that these objects are empty and non-existent, a deep attachment and grasping arises.

<summary>This page explains the second and third phases of the development of the deluded mind, focusing on how intellectual discrimination leads to a continuous cycle of pleasure, pain, and rebirth. It details the transition from simple perception to the deep-seated attachment that binds sentient beings to samsara.</summary>
<keywords>continuity, intellectual cognition, suffering and pleasure, karma, birth and death, grasping, emptiness, Buddhist psychology</keywords>

<note>The following section explains the structure of the reply, consisting of three parts: stating the number of reasons, explaining their characteristics, and providing a summary.</note>

translations.T1:
In terms of the relative importance of the root and the branch, if we speak of action, then action is heavy. Therefore, in this chapter, action comes first, while the subsequent text puts the root before the branch. If we speak in terms of the sequence of knowledge and action, then literature <note>or "the study of texts"</note> comes first. Therefore, the chapter on the four teachings places literature first, followed by action. By examining these two chapters together, it can be seen that literature and action must be pursued in parallel.

○ Zixia said: To appreciate the virtuous as we appreciate beauty, to exert one's full strength in serving one's parents, to be willing to sacrifice one's life in serving one's ruler, and to be sincere in one's words when interacting with friends—even if one says this person has not yet learned, I would certainly call them learned.

Zixia was a disciple of Confucius, surnamed Bu, named Shang, and a man of Wei. To "appreciate the virtuous as we appreciate beauty" means to change one's heart, which prefers physical beauty, to instead prefer virtue with sincerity. The *Collected Commentaries* <note>original: "集註" referring to the *Collected Commentaries on the Analects*</note> ask: How should we interpret this? Seeing the virtuous and changing one’s tendency toward beauty is a matter of turning one's love of beauty toward a love of virtue. Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi</note> said: The two passages regarding "not having seen one who loves virtue as much as one loves beauty" and the *Doctrine of the Mean* both treat distancing oneself from physical beauty as the way to virtue. "Exert" means to relinquish. "Relinquishing one's life" means not to hold on to one's own body or life. This is the sincerity of changing one's love of beauty. Therefore, Master Fan’s explanation is the superior one.

Master Zi Xia said: "If a person values worthiness so as to replace his desire for physical beauty <note>or "changes his expression/demeanor"</note>; if he can exhaust his strength in serving his parents; if he can devote his very life to serving his prince; and if, in his dealings with friends, his words are trustworthy; even if it is said that he has not yet studied, I would certainly say that he has."

Zi Xia was a disciple of Confucius, surnamed Bu and named Shang, a man of Wei. To "value worthiness" <term>xian xian</term> <gloss>to treat the worthy as worthy</gloss> means to replace the heart that loves beauty with a sincere love for goodness. The Collected Commentaries <note>the *Jizhu* by Zhu Xi</note> ask: how can seeing worthiness change one’s outward appearance? This refers to the sincerity of loving goodness. Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi</note> remarked that twice it has been said "I have not seen one who loves virtue as he loves beauty." The *Doctrine of the Mean* also considers distancing oneself from beauty as a method. To "devote" <term>zhi</term> <gloss>to hand over or commit</gloss> one's body means to give oneself up entirely, not holding one's life as one’s own. Since this involves the sincerity of replacing the love of beauty, Fan’s explanation is the most excellent.

The Lord Buddha addressed Subhuti, saying: "What think you? If a disciple, having obtained all the treasures of this universe, were to bestow these in the exercise of charity, would such a disciple consequently enjoy a considerable merit?" Subhuti assenting, said: "Honoured of the Worlds! such a disciple would consequently enjoy a very considerable merit."

The Lord Buddha thereupon addressed Subhuti, saying: "If there were any real or permanent quality in merit, the Lord Buddha would not have spoken of such merit as 'considerable.' It is because there is neither a tangible nor material quality in merit, that the Lord Buddha referred to the merit of that disciple as 'considerable.'"

The Lord Buddha addressed Subhuti, saying: "What think you? Can the Lord Buddha be perceived by means of his perfect material body?" Subhuti replied, saying: "Honoured of the Worlds! it is improbable that the Lord Buddha can be perceived by means of his perfect material body. And why? Because, what the Lord Buddha referred to as a 'perfect material body,' is not in reality a 'perfect material body,' it is merely termed a 'perfect material body.'"

->The undefiled, pure light,
The sun of wisdom that shatters all darkness,
Can subdue the disasters of wind and fire,
And brilliantly illuminate the world.<-

->With a body of compassion like the thunder of precepts,
And a mind of loving-kindness like a great, wondrous cloud,
Pouring down the sweet rain of the Dharma,
To extinguish the flames of affliction.<-

->In disputes before officials,
Or in the terror of the battlefield,
If one calls upon the power of Avalokiteshvara <note>original: "觀世音"</note>,
All enemies will retreat and disperse.<-

->The wondrous voice, the voice of the world-observer,
The Brahma-voice, the voice like the rising tide,
Surpasses all sounds of the world;
Therefore, one must constantly keep it in mind.<-

->In every thought, do not harbor doubt.
Avalokiteshvara, the pure and holy one,
In the midst of suffering, agony, disaster, and death,
Can serve as a refuge and protector.<-

->Possessing all virtues,
Looking upon all beings with eyes of compassion,
An ocean of accumulated blessings beyond measure;
Therefore, one should bow in reverence.<-
